ith all the recent advancements in large language models, full research access to them remains limited because of the resources that are required to train and run such large models. This restricted access has limited researchers’ ability to understand how and why these large language models work, hindering progress on efforts to improve their robustness and mitigate known issues, such as bias, toxicity, and the potential for generating misinformation.

Smaller models trained on more tokens — which are pieces of words — are easier to retrain and fine-tune for specific potential product use cases. We trained LLaMA 65B and LLaMA 33B on 1.4 trillion tokens. Our smallest model, LLaMA 7B, is trained on one trillion tokens.

Like other large language models, LLaMA works by taking a sequence of words as an input and predicts a next word to recursively generate text. To train our model, we chose text from the 20 languages with the most speakers, focusing on those with Latin and Cyrillic alphabets.

There is still more research that needs to be done to [address the risks of bias](https://ai.facebook.com/blog/measure-fairness-and-mitigate-ai-bias/), toxic comments, and hallucinations in large language models. Like other models, LLaMA shares these challenges. As a foundation model, LLaMA is designed to be versatile and can be applied to many different use cases, versus a fine-tuned model that is designed for a specific task. By sharing the code for LLaMA, other researchers can more easily test new approaches to limiting or eliminating these problems in large language models. We also provide in the paper a set of evaluations on benchmarks evaluating model biases and toxicity to show the model’s limitations and to support further research in this crucial area.

To maintain integrity and prevent misuse, we are releasing our model under a noncommercial license focused on research use cases. Access to the model will be granted on a case-by-case basis to academic researchers; those affiliated with organizations in government, civil society, and academia; and industry research laboratories around the world. People interested in applying for access can find the link to the application in our research paper.

We believe that the entire AI community — academic researchers, civil society, policymakers, and industry — must work together to develop clear guidelines around responsible AI in general and responsible large language models in particular. We look forward to seeing what the community can learn — and eventually build — using LLaMA.

Title: Introducing the Model Context Protocol

Markdown Content:
Today, we're open-sourcing the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) (MCP), a new standard for connecting AI assistants to the systems where data lives, including content repositories, business tools, and development environments. Its aim is to help frontier models produce better, more relevant responses.

As AI assistants gain mainstream adoption, the industry has invested heavily in model capabilities, achieving rapid advances in reasoning and quality. Yet even the most sophisticated models are constrained by their isolation from data—trapped behind information silos and legacy systems. Every new data source requires its own custom implementation, making truly connected systems difficult to scale.

MCP addresses this challenge. It provides a universal, open standard for connecting AI systems with data sources, replacing fragmented integrations with a single protocol. The result is a simpler, more reliable way to give AI systems access to the data they need.

The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that enables developers to build secure, two-way connections between their data sources and AI-powered tools. The architecture is straightforward: developers can either expose their data through MCP servers or build AI applications (MCP clients) that connect to these servers.

Today, we're introducing three major components of the Model Context Protocol for developers:

*   The Model Context Protocol [specification and SDKs](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol)
*   Local MCP server support in the [Claude Desktop apps](https://claude.ai/redirect/website.v1.e1970a08-9791-46d6-920c-93bcbafea97d/download)

The Sora web and app experiences were discontinued on April 26, 2026.

The Sora API will be discontinued on September 24, 2026.

Yes, you can export your data following the steps [below](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001152-what-to-know-about-the-sora-discontinuation#how-can-i-access-and-export-content-i-created-in-sora). If a final export window is offered, we’ll notify you by email before it begins. **We recommend you export your Sora content as soon as possible.**

## What happens to my data after the Sora app is discontinued?

After Sora is discontinued, and after the period of time of any final export window passes (if we are able to offer one), we will permanently delete any data associated with your use of Sora.

## How can I access and export content I created in Sora?

You can export content you created in Sora by going to [sora.chatgpt.com/sunset](https://sora.chatgpt.com/sunset) and clicking on **Export**. You'll get an email when it's ready.

Initial assessment requires understanding the Arc's specific arguments regarding open versus closed AI systems. Focus must remain on factual accuracy and interpretation of presented arguments, within the specified baseline and cutoff. The aim is to assess the Arc's claims independently according to the defined editorial standards.


Legacy anchor events are distinct from new Arc sources; quoted statements require independent verification. Broken legacy links are not fixed by new Arc sources. The analysis must separate claim support, source origin, prose, Arc v2.4 eligibility and human approval. Review chapters for PASS_DRAFT / REVISE / HOLD with specific changes, checking for unsupported claims and vendor statement repetition, then provide Arc-level verdicts, shadow environment and publication eligibility.


The structure suggests a chronological progression of AI accessibility, starting with service-based access and moving towards downloadable models and market reactions. Evaluating these chapters requires analyzing the cited sources for corroboration of the claims. The geopolitical chapter warrants close examination for potential restrictions and their impact on open versus closed models. It is necessary to identify and verify the relationship between anchor events and cited sources.


The Arc's metadata validates against the specified criteria: chapter count, anchor event distribution per chapter and total count, the temporal scope of anchor events, and event publication status are all confirmed. The related arc link is non-self-referential. Excerpts are explicitly partial captures.


Examining the evidence suggests early AI releases emphasized service-based access, like APIs and hosted platforms, rather than model downloads. These early examples, while differing in details, share a common architecture based on service-based access. Considering that this is not a monolithic definition, I will explore the distinctions between varying access models, as "closed" does not automatically mean the same restrictions for each product.


Chapter 1 sources are vendor announcements; therefore, they only validate the offered access model, not independent performance claims. The bilingual alignment is confirmed, leading to a "PASS_DRAFT" verdict for Chapter 1.

The narrative shifts to downloadable models. "Stable Diffusion" represents a new model access paradigm.

Meta's LLaMA release demonstrates another model access control mechanism with its restricted license. The unauthorized redistribution is correctly distinguished from permissive open-source release.


Llama 3.1 broadened downloadable weights but clarified that licensing and deployment still restrict usage. The narrative distinguishes between licensed releases, unauthorized redistribution, and commercial availability, cautioning against equating access with open-source status. All sources are primary actor releases, and the cautious narrative avoids unverified vendor claims while highlighting license constraints and deployment costs. The chapter is bilingual and receives a "PASS_DRAFT" verdict.

Chapter 3 describes DeepSeek R1's release, downloadable weights, and related performance and efficiency claims.


DeepSeek's announcement must be treated as a primary vendor claim, requiring independent validation of its performance assertions. The cited Carnegie analysis suggests market reaction was complex, making it difficult to attribute stock fluctuations solely to DeepSeek's release. Training costs are likely understated; the full expenditure includes significant capital investments beyond marginal compute expenses. Furthermore, benchmark comparisons require controlled environments and specified tasks, as Llama 4 and GPT-5 releases are outside the R1 comparison criteria.


DeepSeek's self-reported training costs are separated from independent financial analysis, which highlights the omission of critical capital expenditure. The chapter text is bilingual and is thus marked "PASS_DRAFT".

The US export directive restricting access to Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models is supported by both Anthropic's statement and independent reporting. Z.ai's GLM-5.2 release and DeepSeek V4's prior appearance offer counterpoints to the restrictions, raising questions about geopolitical impact on model accessibility.


The Arc correctly separates temporal sequence from causal relationship, dismissing the direct response claim regarding GLM-5.2 and export controls.  It also highlights the limitations of comparing the models' accessibility.  The Arc accurately distinguishes between different release models and the vendor-reported claims, cautioning against equating access with benchmark performance. The corrected source points to a valid alternative without claiming the original broken source's URL is repaired.


Anthropic's statement is treated as a corroboration of events, not an independent assessment. It's necessary to treat vendor benchmark tables with skepticism, requiring verification. Chapter 4's verdict is "PASS_DRAFT".

The narrative in Chapter 5 examines a move away from binary open/closed models, covering ownership, product continuity, interoperability, and software distribution. These industry events don't establish performance parity between open and proprietary models. Each anchor event requires individual examination to ensure support for any overarching claim.


Examining StepFun's model release, the license explicitly restricts commercial use and requires attribution, differentiating it from uninhibited open-source licensing. This conditional release doesn't confirm independent performance parity or widespread adoption, emphasizing deployment terms. The analysis distinguishes between open weights, defined license restrictions, and verified claims of broad-scale deployment.


The abstract emphasizes the differing access types and cautions against simplistic market analysis and assumptions about model weight significance, focusing instead on user rights and limitations. The conclusion restates the critical distinctions between service access, weight access, and reuse permissions, and summarizes analytical caveats, while suggesting that open and closed models will likely co-exist and require rigorous assessment.


Programmatic checks confirm structural integrity, metadata validation, and anchor presence within the Arc. Semantic claim validity requires manual comparison of quoted excerpts and narrative assertions. Legacy broken URLs are correctly decoupled from the new Arc source, which provides valid supporting evidence. The review is ready for staging environment finalization.

# INDEPENDENT EPOCHARC v2.4 ARC ASSESSMENT

**Review Subject**: Arc `open-vs-closed` ("Open Weights, Closed Services: Paths to AI Access" / "开放权重与封闭服务：AI 的不同访问路径")  
**Baseline Commit**: `d558bde98416edf85cd95cb63905dea65d070010`  
**Evidence Cutoff**: `2026-10-17`  
**Draft Producer Session**: `019f7eb3-bd32-7de0-b812-96efddac7723` (`gpt-6-sol`)  
**Reviewer Session**: Fresh independent evaluation session (`gemini-3.8-independent`)  
**Scope**: Entire bilingual Arc (Abstract, 5 Chapters, Conclusion, Metadata, Source Mappings)

---

### Disclosure on Evidence Excerpts
As required by v2.4 integrity standards, all source evaluations below are based strictly on the verbatim markdown excerpts and captured metadata provided in the review packet (captured via Jina Reader/HTTP snapshots). These captures represent partial source excerpts and do not constitute full-text or dynamic site verification. No browsing was conducted during this evaluation.

---

## 1. Chapter-by-Chapter Evaluation

### Chapter 1: `closed-default` ("Access Through Services" / "通过服务获取能力")
- **Anchors Evaluated**: `gpt3-2020`, `dall-e-2-2022`, `github-copilot-2022`, `chatgpt-2022`
- **Arc-Specific Sources**: `arc-v24-openai-gpt3-api`, `arc-v24-openai-dalle2`, `arc-v24-github-copilot`, `arc-v24-openai-chatgpt`
- **Claim Support & Evidence Analysis**:
  - *Claim*: GPT-3 was offered via API rather than a public weights download; DALL·E 2, Copilot, and ChatGPT offered product usage without model weight delivery.
    - *Excerpt Support*: `arc-v24-openai-gpt3-api` shows OpenAI announced an API explicitly contrasting it with open sourcing ("Why did OpenAI choose to release an API instead of open-sourcing the models?"). `arc-v24-openai-dalle2`, `arc-v24-github-copilot`, and `arc-v24-openai-chatgpt` document hosted web/IDE/service releases without weight downloads.
  - *Vendor Statements vs. Independent Reporting*: All four cited sources are primary launch announcements (`primary_actor`). The narrative accurately scopes them as evidence of the *access mechanisms offered by vendors*, avoiding any unverified vendor performance claims.
  - *Counter-Evidence & Nuance*: The narrative explicitly warns against monolithic categorizations ("calling them all 'closed' can obscure those differences") and refuses to assert that compute constraints alone dictated the delivery models or that no downloadable models existed in that period.
- **Bilingual Consistency**: English and Chinese narratives and insights are closely aligned without drift.
- **Verdict**: **PASS_DRAFT** (No changes required).

---

### Chapter 2: `the-fork-appears` ("More Routes to Downloadable Models" / "获取可下载模型的更多路径")
- **Anchors Evaluated**: `stable-diffusion-2022`, `llama-2023`, `llama-3.1-405b-2024`
- **Arc-Specific Sources**: `arc-v24-stability-2022`, `arc-v24-meta-llama-2023`, `arc-v24-meta-llama31`
- **Claim Support & Evidence Analysis**:
  - *Claim*: Stable Diffusion provided downloadable weights to run image generation locally; Meta provided original LLaMA under a restricted non-commercial research license (distinguished from unauthorized leaks); Llama 3.1 405B expanded downloadable weights, but license terms and deployment compute remain constraints.
    - *Excerpt Support*: `arc-v24-stability-2022` directly links weights/model card on Hugging Face and specifies VRAM requirements (6.9 GB). `arc-v24-meta-llama-2023` confirms release under a "noncommercial license focused on research use cases" granted on a case-by-case basis. `arc-v24-meta-llama31` confirms public weight release of the 405B dense model.
  - *Vendor Statements vs. Independent Reporting*: Sources are primary announcements. The prose treats Meta’s claims of being the "first frontier-level open source AI model" with appropriate editorial distance, correctly emphasizing the legal and technical boundaries (licensing conditions and hardware deployment hurdles).
  - *Counter-Evidence & Nuance*: Evaluates the crucial distinction between research access, leaks/unauthorized copying, and permissive open-source licensing.
- **Bilingual Consistency**: Exact semantic equivalence across EN and ZH texts.
- **Verdict**: **PASS_DRAFT** (No changes required).

---

### Chapter 3: `efficiency-shock` ("Capability Claims and a Market Reaction" / "性能主张与市场反应")
- **Anchors Evaluated**: `deepseek-r1-2025`, `llama-4-2025`, `gpt5-2025`
- **Arc-Specific Sources**: `arc-v24-deepseek-r1`, `arc-v24-carnegie-deepseek-market`, `arc-v24-meta-llama4`, `arc-v24-openai-gpt5`
- **Claim Support & Evidence Analysis**:
  - *Claim*: DeepSeek released R1 with downloadable weights under MIT license alongside self-reported reasoning benchmarks and training efficiency; Nvidia's stock selloff occurred days later; training cost figures reported by vendors do not reflect total system expenditures under standardized accounting; Llama 4 and GPT-5 represent chronological reference releases rather than controlled direct benchmark comparisons.
    - *Excerpt Support*: `arc-v24-deepseek-r1` verifies the MIT license and DeepSeek's self-reported "on par with OpenAI-o1" claims. `arc-v24-carnegie-deepseek-market` (independent Tier 2 analysis) verifies the market turmoil, questions compute-heavy investment theses, and specifically corroborates the accounting distinction: DeepSeek’s cost claims capture marginal training compute while excluding data center buildouts, hardware acquisition, and team expenditures. `arc-v24-meta-llama4` and `arc-v24-openai-gpt5` verify subsequent model releases.
  - *Vendor Statements vs. Independent Reporting*: The narrative scrupulously distinguishes vendor-reported benchmarks and compute claims (`arc-v24-deepseek-r1`) from independent financial/technical analysis (`arc-v24-carnegie-deepseek-market`).
  - *Counter-Evidence & Nuance*: Thoroughly addresses causal fallacies. The text explicitly disclaims single-cause attribution for the market drop ("timing and commentary cannot establish how much of the price change the release caused").
- **Bilingual Consistency**: Fully aligned in tone, caveats, and factual precision.
- **Verdict**: **PASS_DRAFT** (No changes required).

---

### Chapter 4: `geopolitical-twist` ("Access Restrictions and Alternative Releases" / "访问限制与其他发布")
- **Anchors Evaluated**: `claude-fable-ban-2026`, `glm-52-open-source-2026`, `deepseek-v4-2026`
- **Arc-Specific Sources**: `arc-v24-anthropic-fable-statement`, `arc-v24-verge-fable`, `arc-v24-glm52-corrected`, `arc-v24-deepseek-v4`
- **Claim Support & Evidence Analysis**:
  - *Claim*: In June 2026, a US export control directive restricted foreign access to Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5; Z.ai released GLM-5.2 weights shortly thereafter; DeepSeek V4 was released in April 2026; temporal proximity does not prove the export ban caused the Chinese releases; vendor benchmarks and cost claims do not independently prove frontier parity.
    - *Excerpt Support*: `arc-v24-anthropic-fable-statement` (primary) and `arc-v24-verge-fable` (independent reporting) document the June 12, 2026 export control directive and subsequent worldwide shutdown. `arc-v24-glm52-corrected` confirms GLM-5.2 model card under MIT license on Hugging Face. `arc-v24-deepseek-v4` confirms April 24, 2026 release of V4-Pro and V4-Flash.
  - *Vendor Statements vs. Independent Reporting*: The narrative explicitly notes that GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek V4 benchmark scores and low per-token pricing are company-reported, refusing to treat them as certified parity with closed frontier models.
  - *Counter-Evidence & Nuance*: Directly refutes simplistic geopolitical narratives. Unlike the legacy anchor text for `glm-52-open-source-2026` which asserted a direct response, this chapter narrative adheres to v2.4 rules by affirming that chronological sequence cannot establish causal policy reversals, nor does the availability of an alternative prove that export controls were ineffective.
- **Bilingual Consistency**: High precision in English and Chinese across diplomatic and technical terminology.
- **Verdict**: **PASS_DRAFT** (No changes required).

---

### Chapter 5: `fork-ahead` ("More Than a Binary Choice" / "不只是二选一")
- **Anchors Evaluated**: `openai-pbc-restructure-2025`, `mcp-protocol-2024`, `sora-shutdown-2026`, `openclaw-2026`, `stepfun-step-5-preview-open-weights-2026`
- **Arc-Specific Sources**: `arc-v24-openai-pbc-cnbc`, `arc-v24-anthropic-mcp`, `arc-v24-openai-sora`, `arc-v24-openclaw-official`, `arc-v24-stepfun-license`, `arc-v24-stepfun-license-full`
- **Claim Support & Evidence Analysis**:
  - *Claim*: The landscape cannot be reduced to open vs. closed; OpenAI's PBC restructuring, Sora's discontinuation, MCP, and OpenClaw illustrate governance, lifecycle, interoperability, and distribution layers; StepFun released Step 5 Preview weights on October 15 under Model License 1.0; the license requires attribution and commercial licensing under specific thresholds; available weights do not equate to unencumbered open-source rights, verified capability parity, or widespread production use.
    - *Excerpt Support*: `arc-v24-openai-pbc-cnbc` confirms OpenAI Group PBC conversion and corporate structure. `arc-v24-anthropic-mcp` establishes MCP as an open protocol for tool integration. `arc-v24-openai-sora` details the sunset dates (web/app on April 26, 2026; API on September 24, 2026). `arc-v24-openclaw-official` confirms OpenClaw's local execution and 501(c)(3) governance. `arc-v24-stepfun-license` and `arc-v24-stepfun-license-full` establish the self-hosted inference support while verifying the license restrictions (Section 2(b) attribution required at >100M MAU or >$20M revenue; Section 2(c) commercial license required for hardware OEMs or MaaS operators >$20M revenue).
  - *Vendor Statements vs. Independent Reporting*: The legal text of StepFun Model License 1.0 is analyzed directly as a primary legal instrument. StepFun's performance assertions are properly classified as vendor claims that lack independent replication.
  - *Counter-Evidence & Nuance*: Thoroughly breaks the false binary of "open vs closed" by showing that downloadable weights often arrive with commercial and attribution restrictions, and that weight availability is distinct from actual enterprise adoption.
- **Bilingual Consistency**: Complete parity between English and Chinese terminology.
- **Verdict**: **PASS_DRAFT** (No changes required).

---

## 2. Source Lineage & Legacy Debt Audit

1. **Resolution of GLM-5.2 Source Discrepancy**:
   - The legacy anchor `glm-52-open-source-2026` contained a dead URL (`https://huggingface.co/zai/GLM-5.2`), which returned a 404 error during verification.
   - The Arc draft correctly stages and references a new Arc-only source `arc-v24-glm52-corrected` pointing to the live repository (`https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.2`).
   - In accordance with rule **GOV-03**, this new Arc source supports the Arc narrative but **does not alter or repair the legacy anchor's source record**. The legacy baseline remains untouched, and no historical re-audit is claimed.
2. **Origin ID and Republication Integrity**:
   - Primary company statements and third-party news reports maintain distinct and accurate `originId` attributes (e.g., `openai-gpt3-api-2020`, `zai-glm52-weights-2026`, `the-verge-fable-negotiations-2026`).
   - Republished vendor claims in third-party news are not counted as independent capability verifications.

---

## 3. Structural & Editorial Standards Compliance (ARC-01, ARC-MODEL, LANG-01/02)

| Criteria | Policy Requirement | Current Arc Value | Status |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Chapter Count** | 3 to 6 chapters | 5 chapters | **PASS** |
| **Anchors per Chapter** | 2 to 5 anchors | Ch1: 4, Ch2: 3, Ch3: 3, Ch4: 3, Ch5: 5 | **PASS** |
| **Total Distinct Anchors**| $\ge 5$ anchors | 18 unique anchors | **PASS** |
| **Anchor Temporal Span** | $\ge 3$ years | 2020 (`gpt3-2020`) to 2026 (`stepfun...`) = 6 years | **PASS** |
| **Anchor Event Status** | All anchors must be `published` | All 18 anchors are published in the dataset | **PASS** |
| **Related Arcs** | Non-empty, no self-ref, published | `["transformer-empire"]` | **PASS** |
| **Language Parity** | Strict fact/claim alignment | EN and ZH texts match in facts, dates, caveats, and terms | **PASS** |
| **Counter-Evidence** | Must evaluate counter-evidence | Evaluated in all chapters (market causes, licensing limits, geopolitics) | **PASS** |

---

## 4. Overall Arc Verdict & Publication Determinations

### Arc-Level Prose Verdict
The draft for `open-vs-closed` represents an exemplary implementation of v2.4 narrative guidelines. Rather than presenting a simplistic or partisan story of "open-source triumph" or "proprietary dominance," it meticulously disentangles three distinct concepts: **service availability**, **weight accessibility**, and **legal redistribution rights**. It consistently treats vendor benchmarks as unverified claims, explicitly notes where market movements cannot be causally attributed to model releases, and dissects conditional licenses (such as StepFun's Model License 1.0) to demonstrate that modern AI access models exist on a complex spectrum.
